cues.text: Physician Turned Bishop
According to tradition, Blaise practiced medicine at Sebaste , in the Roman province of Armenia (modern Sivas, Turkey), before being chosen bishop of the city.
The Catholic Encyclopedia notes with characteristic caution, 'all the particulars concerning his life and martyrdom which are found in the Acts are purely legendary.'
It allows that Blaise was very likely a genuine bishop martyred in the early fourth century.
Arrested in a Wilderness Cave

When persecution under Emperor Licinius reached Armenia around 316, Blaise withdrew into the wilderness and took shelter in a remote cave, where wild animals reportedly gathered peacefully around him.
The governor's hunters, searching the countryside for beasts to supply the amphitheater, discovered him there and brought him back for trial.
The Choking Boy
While imprisoned awaiting judgment, tradition holds that Blaise was approached by a distraught mother whose young son was choking to death on a fishbone lodged in his throat.
The bishop laid hands on the boy, or in another version of the story blessed him with two crossed candles, and the child was miraculously healed.
This episode gave rise to the enduring association between St. Blaise and protection of the throat.
Torture and Martyrdom
Blaise was subjected to severe torture, traditionally said to include being torn with iron combs used for carding wool, before finally being beheaded.
The Acts also record the martyrdom of seven women alongside him, arrested for gathering up drops of his blood during his torment.
The Blessing of Throats
Devotion to Blaise as a healer of throat ailments spread from the Christian East by the sixth century and reached the Latin West by the ninth.

It eventually gave rise to the still-practiced Blessing of the Throats , in which a priest holds two crossed candles to a person's throat on or near Blaise's feast day, invoking his intercession against choking and disease.
Legacy
Blaise became one of the medieval Fourteen Holy Helpers , a group of saints especially invoked for particular bodily needs.

His blessing of throats remains one of the most widely observed sacramental customs in the Catholic Church today, a living link to a physician-bishop about whose actual life almost nothing certain can be historically confirmed.
